missions.title: The Next Bell
missions.knowledgeQuestion: When should a change in evidence change what we tell other people?
missions.stake: If the notice is too sure, or not sure enough, the harbour does not move in time.

objectives.title: Follow the new passage from the Nexus to the Observatory Coast.
Compare the rain at the quay and the headland with Forecaster Neri.
Read the model chart and decide how to carry its limit into the notice.
Choose how to send the notice with Signalkeeper Ruan.
Read the headland rain gauge at the next bell.
Help Ruan update the notice using the new headland reading.
Take the two named gauge readings to Ruan’s next crew.

missions.title: A Copy Past the Sheds
missions.knowledgeQuestion: Whose route does an official message assume?

objectives.title: Find the route that misses a notice and help Ruan reach it.

missions.title: Two Ways to Count a Bell
missions.knowledgeQuestion: What can change when a local way of counting travels with a record?

objectives.title: Help the apprentice pass on the timed gauge slip.

missions.title: Clear for Whom?
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How do the checks behind a word change what another person can infer?

objectives.title: Try the menders’ ribbon at the tagged row and the unmarked edge.
Check the lookout’s mark with the rain gauge, then put both meanings where the crews can find them.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: I’ve been handed two notices. One says the rain is holding off. The other says it’s coming down hard. If I nail up just one, half the quay will tell me I’ve never looked out a window.

options.text: Where did the reports come from?
Who is waiting for the notice?
I’ll go and look.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: One hand was here, under the lee of the quay wall. One was up with Neri on the headland. Start with our gauge. Keep its place next to its number.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The cutters read the board while they sort their lines. Basket crews wait at the stone steps, out of sight of it. Both want to know which report applies to their bit of coast.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: My sleeve is drenched. Ruan sent word that the quay barely felt it. The headland gauge is beside the chart case. Read it and bring the quay reading so we can compare the same bell.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: Five at Wind Peg, where the lookout shift meets. Two at Wallfoot, where the basket crews put down their loads. My register calls them exposed headland and sheltered quay. Both gauges stood out for one station bell. A new runner needs the names people use when they give directions.

options.text: Put both readings on the same dated strip.
Pin each reading to the place it belongs.
Give me a moment.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: Wallfoot goes beside the two. Wind Peg goes beside the five. Keep both work names level with their register names and figures. The apprentice can read the whole strip at once. There’s a tray beside my bench to send it down.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: A new runner took headland to mean the whole hill. I’ve put the names by the gauges. Follow the lookout rail to Wind Peg and the edge of the sea wall to Wallfoot. Then Ruan can give the runner a walking guide.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: This strip keeps both of the first readings together. Each line has a register name and the name you’ll hear on that shift. Ruan’s rack is beside the quay workbench.

options.text: Wrap the dated strip for Ruan’s rack.
Leave the tray for now.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: The two names stay with the two rows. The strip is ready for the shelf by Ruan.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: My apprentice can compare both figures while they unpack the basket tally. Leave me room beside the strip. I can show a visitor the route to either gauge.

options.text: Lay the paired readings on the working rack.
Keep the strip with me for now.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: They found the two and the five in one look. Next they can take a visitor to the real place. People ask for Wallfoot by name when they step off a boat.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The wall ends at Wallfoot. The lookout rail ends at Wind Peg. Our new runner can check each reading where it stood. The runner will make two stops, so give them the route before they set out.

options.text: Hang the walking guide on the crossing hook.
Leave the hook for now.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: They called back ‘Wallfoot’ on the way past, so I knew which gauge they’d checked. They’ll read Wind Peg with the lookout on the next stop.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: There’s a second piece of paper on the chart table. The gauge sheets say what fell. The chart has our estimate for the next bell. Take a look at the two papers before we send anything.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: The chart carries the same wind into the next bell. It can help people plan if that holds. If we put the sheet up on its own, someone will copy the forecast as a fresh reading.

options.text: Put the estimate on a separate strip and keep its wind condition.
Put the readings first and mark when we’ll test the estimate again.
Hold the copy here for a moment.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: I’ll tie the condition to the estimate. If the wind changes, Ruan can take down that one strip without losing the two readings.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: I’ve left a space for the next bell. The estimate stays with its wind condition, and readers can see when we’ll have a fresh number.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: Ruan needs the notice now. I can check the headland gauge again at the next bell. Ask Ruan which route to send your copy along.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The readings and the forecast are separate on your copy. Good. The tide is turning and I only have one hand free. I can pin the sheet on the board or send a runner to the steps before the basket crews leave.

options.text: Pin the qualified notice on the quay board.
Send the runner to the basket crews with the written copy.
I’ll wait a moment.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The cutters can read the condition alongside the numbers. The board is also a place to check back. I heard the basket crews call from the steps. They’ll need another way to see it.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The runner has the copy in hand. I’ve asked for the estimate and its condition to be read together. The steps will hear first. The copy must come back here when there’s a new reading.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The next bell rang while you were here. Neri should have a new headland reading by now. Bring it back so we can tell people what changed.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: There’s a new line at the gauge. Down from five, and the interval was one bell again. I left the quay column open. Until it comes in, we only know what the headland measured.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The people at the board have seen our first copy. One has drawn a line in the margin where the new numbers ought to go. The next bell gave us two at the headland, with no fresh quay mark. I have one signed catch. A crew with it can attach its own dated check to the correction. The other crew can send a signed slip back for me to attach.

options.text: Pin the new reading beside the earlier notice, with the quay entry left open. Lend the catch to the quay cutters.
Pin the new reading at the board. Send the signed catch to the basket crews at the steps.
I’ll leave the board for now.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The basket crews heard us at the steps first. Our runner is back. The second headland mark is two, and the quay’s second line is still missing. I have one signed catch. A crew with it can attach its own dated check to the correction. The other crew can send a signed slip back for me to attach.

options.text: Send the runner back with the new reading and leave a dated copy here. Lend the catch to the basket crews at the steps.
Send the runner back with the corrected sheet. Leave the signed catch with the quay cutters.
I’ll leave the copy for now.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The board holds both notices. The cutters can attach a dated check at the quay hook under my eye. The basket crews can ask me to attach theirs.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The runner takes the dated headland reading and the signed catch to the steps. The basket crews can add their own check there. The quay copy stays here, and I’ll attach the cutters’ signed slip if they bring it.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The board has its dated correction. I’ve lent the catch to the basket crews at the steps. They can add a check there themselves. I’ll attach the cutters’ signed slip if they bring it here.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The runner has the correction for the basket crews. The quay cutters keep the catch at their hook. They can add a check there themselves. The runner can bring me any signed reply from the steps.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A cutter holds Ruan’s signed catch. The correction still has an open line for Wallfoot at the second bell. “I can clip our next reading here beside his when we have one. His reply can go beside it. Can you fit the dated blank under the catch?”

options.text: Fit the dated blank at the cutters’ hook and leave the reading line open.
Read the signed catch again.
Leave the catch for later.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The cutters can now post a dated field check for everyone at the quay. The marked blank still waits for a second quay reading. The basket crews can bring Ruan their check in person.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The basket crews’ checker turns Ruan’s signed catch toward the steps. The copy says two at Wind Peg for the second bell. Wallfoot’s second line is empty. “If our next run brings a reading, I want to pin its time here, where people can see it.”

options.text: Fit the dated blank under the basket crews’ catch at the steps.
Read the signed catch again.
Leave the catch for later.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The checker can now pin a named, dated reading beside the notice where the crews stop. The second Wallfoot line stays open until they actually have a reading. The cutters can still leave their check with Ruan.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: Thank you. Every time a bell rings someone points at the old line, then reads the new one. Keep the first where they can see it.

options.text: A path by the sheds misses the notice. Could a copy go at the crossing?
I’ll look around the quay.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: The runner has come back with word. The crews remembered the figure. They went back to the copy for the place. I’m glad we kept both together.

options.text: A path by the sheds misses the notice. Could a copy go at the crossing?
I’ll look around the quay.

dialogue.speaker: coast-signalkeeper
dialogue.text: I can use the crossing that both crews pass. People down here call their change of shift a bell, so I’ll write “station bell” by our readings. That way a crew can tell whose clock the notice follows.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: We can compare what fell for two bells at the headland. The quay line is still open for the next observer. I’m leaving this sheet beside the model so the next person can see which is which.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: A landing apprentice holds the gauge slip beside the basket crews’ work book. The headland rings its bell to mark each timed reading. On the quay, crews say “a bell” for a turn carrying baskets. A visiting crew has copied “one bell” and put it beside the wrong mark.

options.text: Leave both ways of counting and add the two station bell marks.
Stamp the two station bell marks on the copy. Keep the quay phrase in its book.
Leave the slip for now.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The apprentice clips the slip to the work book. The quay crews keep their way of counting turns. A visitor follows the station marks to the exact span used for the gauge.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The visitor takes the stamped copy to the headland. It has a start and finish anyone at the station can check. The quay work book keeps its own phrase for the next crew.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The net-menders set aside this practice frame for the next crew. Their tag says ‘clear’ beside one repaired row. An apprentice reads that as a check of the whole frame. The same blue ribbon can pass through either place.

options.text: Pass the ribbon through the tagged row.
Pass the same ribbon along the unmarked edge.
Keep the two readings with their places on the frame.
Leave the frame here.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The blue ribbon passes through the tagged row. The test follows the place the menders marked.

options.text: Pass the same ribbon along the unmarked edge.
Keep the two readings with their places on the frame.
Leave the ribbon at the row.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The same ribbon catches at the unmarked edge. The frame stayed fixed when you moved that one ribbon. The checked row and the edge can give different results.

options.text: Pass the ribbon through the tagged row.
Keep the two readings with their places on the frame.
Leave the ribbon at the edge.

dialogue.speaker: narrator
dialogue.text: The menders leave a strip by each place so the next crew sees which row passed. ‘Clear’ is their word for a place they have checked. The station lookout has put the same word on a sight mark. Go see what the lookout was checking.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: The menders checked a row and the lookout checked a view. The tower was visible when the interval ended. The gauge still held five finger-widths of rain from that interval. Our next runner serves both crews. Should each crew keep its own caption, or should the runner carry one card naming both checks?

options.text: Leave separate tags at the frame and lookout. Let each crew update its own check.
Give the runner a folded copy naming both crews and both places.
Read the frame and lookout tags again.
Read the runner’s joined copy again.
Leave the checks here for now.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: A mender can update the row tag where they do the work. The lookout keeps the sight mark beside the rain record. A runner can check either at its own place. A person moving between crews may need to visit both records.

dialogue.speaker: coast-forecaster
dialogue.text: The runner reads the menders’ row to the next crew before they try the edge. At the board, they name the lookout and the time of the sight mark. A person crossing between crews can compare both uses in one place. The card needs a fresh mark when either crew reports again.

hints.text: There is an invitation at the Nexus.
The Conservators leave the invitation when their exhibition opens.
Return to the Nexus after publishing the Preserved Lives exhibition.
Use the Observatory Coast passage in the Nexus.
A wet sleeve tells you something about one place.
The quay keeper and the headland observer used the same interval.
Read the two rain gauges. One is at the harbour and one is by the station.
After reading both gauges, talk to Neri at the station. Choose how to record the contrast.
The people at each gauge use the landmark they pass on shift.
Neri has left a tray for paired readings or two tags by the gauge landmarks, depending on your choice.
Pick up the dated strip at the station or check the Wind Peg and Wallfoot tags at their gauges. Ruan has a place for each kind of copy.
Deliver the wrapped strip to the shelf beside Ruan, or check both landmark tags and hang the guide on the hook by the harbour crossing.
The chart is a sketch of what might happen next.
Which condition does the forecast assume? Find it on the chart.
Read the model chart at the station. Ask Neri how much of the forecast can travel.
With the readings compared, talk to Neri after reading the chart. Pick a way to keep its scope in the notice.
The harbour has two ways of getting a message past the quay.
One reaches people at the board. The other reaches people waiting by the steps.
Return to Signalkeeper Ruan with Neri’s qualified forecast.
Ask Ruan to use the board or send the runner. The message keeps the chart’s limit either way.
Neri’s estimate was for the next interval. It needs another reading.
A second mark has arrived from the headland. The quay has not reported again.
Return to the station after sending the notice.
Read the new observation by the headland gauge. Keep the missing quay reading in mind.
A later observation can change what you tell people now.
A change at the headland still leaves the quay uncertain.
Take the next headland reading back to Ruan in the harbour.
Post a dated correction for whichever channel carried the first notice.
The carriers do not all pass the same place.
Check the harbour notebook for the path past the sheds.
Find the notebook near the quay. Bring its note to Ruan after the update.
Ask about the missed copy. Ruan can name the station bell and leave a duplicate where the paths meet.
The quay words have two uses.
Look for the slip just inland from the quay gauge.
Read the apprentice’s slip and the crews’ work book together.
Keep the two station marks so a visitor can check the reading’s interval. There are two places to leave the crews’ words.
The menders’ tag points to part of the frame.
Find the practice frame near the way from the quay to the station.
Compare two places using the same inspection ribbon.
Pass the blue ribbon through the tagged row and try it at the unmarked edge. Keep the locations with what you saw.
The same word can travel ahead of the check it describes.
The lookout’s ‘clear’ mark follows a view of Lantern Tower.
At Headland Station, read the sight mark and rain gauge. Bring the two crew checks to Neri’s board.
Choose separate tags at the frame and lookout or send one card with the runner. Keep the check and place with each use of ‘clear’.

journal.title: The next bell
journal.text: The quay and headland measured the same bell at different places. I sent the readings with a limited estimate, then helped Ruan publish the next headland mark with the second quay line still open.
The cutters can attach their own dated check at the quay. The basket crews still have a route through Ruan. The headland correction keeps an empty line for the next Wallfoot measurement.
The basket crews can attach their own dated check at the steps. The cutters still have a route through Ruan. The headland correction keeps an empty line for the next Wallfoot measurement.

journal.title: The crossing copy
journal.text: A message has a route. At the crossing, the two crews can reach a dated copy and tell which bell came from the station.

journal.title: Clear for whom?
journal.text: The menders’ ‘clear’ names one tested row. The lookout’s ‘clear’ means the tower was visible at the bell. I checked the word with the work it came from, then helped the crews share both checks.

moments.did: You kept a first notice available and changed it when a new observation arrived.
You found a route the first notice missed and made room for those crews to see a copy.
